Not only did Thief decide to reject the supernatural elements of the past games, but they replaced it and the lore with nothing more than a religious zealot who wants to control whatever the hell "primal" is supposed to be and rejected Resident Evil wall crawlers that behave like discount clickers from the last of us. There is no imagination in this game, there is no care or interest or love of the series that came before it. If there were, they wouldn't have systematically rejected every core tennant and game design element of those games. 

You'll spend your entire adventure doing nothing else but walking up behind guards and activating a painfully repetitive takedown animation which is so popular among big budget games today. Because why would simply swing your blackjack and knock out a guard when you could wait for a command prompt to allow you to activate their TOTALLY BAD ASS animation which comes coupled with a sound effect so loud you'd think stealth wasn't a priority. That is one of the most frustrating parts of Thief, the animations tied to every single action you perform, from opening a drawer to picking up a coin, every one of them is paired with this 2 second animation that slows down picking up nickels and dimes to a crawl. In previous Thieves if you were to happen upon a chest with loot, you could pick up everything in that chest in as much time as it would take you to grab a single silver cup in Thief. To add to the frustration, the same command prompt for looting is the same one that locks you into peaking around cornes. You'll find yourself more often than not peering around a desk or shutting a door while you try to loot from a desk or the purse off a guard. 

Strategy is not necessary. In previous Thief games you were given a wide tool set from moss arrows, fire arrows, water arrows, noise maker arrows to rope arrows, however in Thief 4, you'll occassionally use water arrows and absolutely nothing else. There is no tactical use or requirement for any of your equipment. You'll get from the start of the game to the end with just "Press Q to TAKEDOWN", the same guards, over and over and over again. Rope arrows have even been downgraded from sensibly being used on wood surfaces to specifically designated wooden beams with a glowing blue rope tied around it to tell you, "use your rope arrow here to get to this place" which is generally just a single piece of loot or an alternate path which really doesn't change anything in terms of navigation. 

The world design has gone from an realistically designed location to a video gamey linear map that simply gives you a couple of different paths that take you to the same location. You can't get lost, you can't roam, you are given the illusion of an open map while really everything is walled in and blocked off to funnel you to the end. To make matters worse, instaed of a hand drawn map that clues you in as much as Garrett knows about the location, forcing you to become involved in your surroundings and navigate by landmark, they just give you a mini map with quest markers. Despite the fact the levels are basically hallways, they still float indicators all over the screen telling you exactly where to go and exactly where you are. The map alone indicates the greatest reason why Eidos Montreal knows so little or cares so little about Thief and what it is. 

They simply took a popular, respected name in the video game industry and recycled it into this generic, consolized, casualized mess of modern game cliches. At times you'll be running parkour across rooftops while things explode around you and others you'll jarringly be in 3rd person climbing up pipes and grates like Uncharted. They tried to rip off every popular modern game and stir it up into one game because they figured it would return the most profit. It's an incredibly lazy effort, in fact the ending to this game is so empty, you can literally feel the interest of the devs trail off to a roll credit because they just did not care anymore and needed to finish it for release. I could go on and on about all of the ways this game fails not only the Thief name, but game design in general. Eidos Montreal does not get it, they did not care, they cashed in on Thief and left a stain on the integrity of the series. Nothing about the game indicates fans of the series worked on this project. there is nothing about this game that indicates the developers even played the previous games. 

They removed Stephen Russel, the iconic voice of Garrett and replaced him with a generic angsty male that turns this now vampiric, emaciated looking Garrett into any other bland, brooding protagonist. Their excuse for this was they needed a motion cap performance that would sync up with the acting, but nowhere in this game does that ever present as either a necessity or even a feature. There is not a single moment in this game that an actor needed to record his lines while doing motion capture work, further insult to injury, but perhaps its best Stephen Russel was not attached to this poor excuse for a Garrett. 

Bottom line this is a soulless, effortless, completely awful cash grab that did not respect its IP.

Short Review: This is an OK game for $20 or less.

Longer Review:

The problem is at the time of release this was a $60 mess (very buggy) that didn't live up to the franchise (bad story, ignores previous games) and the DLC were straight up predatory, especially the limited use ones.

Looking at the franchise as a whole:

(The original) Thief (1998)(now Thief Gold) was a true milestone at the time of release. It along with other notables like Hitman: Codename 47 and a few others were the early years of stealth gaming. The concept was brilliant and while the level design was rudimentary and the combat was tacked on the game overall just worked and the story was a backdrop to the action (stealing) which is what you were really there for. However, nostalgia glasses off: it's an ugly, wonky old mess of a game that is really hard to play again after all these years. The memories are better than the experience of playing it again. 

Thief 2: The Metal Age (2000) is a real gem, the engine is much more polished, the level design is still the standard that thief games should be compared with and the modding community added 100's of more levels beyond the core game to the experience. Thief 2 is what all future thief games should have tried to improve on.

Thief (3): Deadly Shadows (2004). I had a lot of fun with this on console, unfortunately that's exactly what it was, a console game. It suffered greatly from what is known as "consolitis" where you can ultimately feel how much smaller all the locations were and how dumbed down the game play was. Was it fun? Yea, but honestly it was smaller, shorter and much more limited than Thief 2 was. Good but not really an upgrade in the way fans wanted. They even tried to tack on "open world" but it simply didn't work, you just had tiny city zones with nearly nothing to do in them wasting your time between missions.

Thief (4) (2014) is effectively a reboot, it ignores entirely the previous games and just borrows the characters name and a similar setting. It emulates 3 in trying to have an open world, and while larger it still suffers much of the same problems: small zones, and then somehow makes it worse by cutting you off from them as you make progress. The story rather than being a backdrop to your activity is now front and center, unfortunately it's not well written and the characters you are supposed to care about fall flat while the rest are cliche cutouts. 

What Thief (2014) does well is improve the look and feel, it's a very pretty game. (well, by 2014 standards anyway). By itself it isn't terrible, there's a lot of fun to be had in the puzzles and the stealing. What mars the experience is everything around it from the pointless city zones to the god awful story.

Add to that the abusive DLC on launch day, the absolute buggy mess at full price that took nearly a year post-launch to be playable for many people even with decent systems and the game deserved to be slammed when it came out.

Now? It's playable, it's kinda fun, and picked up at $20 or less… well, at least it's a modern thief game.

/Rant On:
This isn't the way to do open world games and quite frankly thief didn't need to be open world in the first place, the design itself is flawed as all the resources spent on creating a terrible city experience could have gone into designing more and better missions.

We don't need to experience the home life and street wandering, it should be large set piece locations to explore and steal from mission by mission. And the story really shouldn't be driving the experience, we're here to be thieves, the story in 1 and 2 were something that you fell into while trying to just be a thief, it wasn't the point of what you were doing.

There's a lot of functional quality of life improvements in this engine, but the delivery is underwhelming and disrespectful to the fan base as a whole.

What could/should have been:

A thief game with a modern engine, no open world nonsense, big theme-park zones for each mission with tons of things to steal, level designer and mod support so the community could keep making more and varied missions, a story that respected the previous games and didn't get in the way of game play, basically everything that 2 was but in a modern package and quality of life upgrades.

I doubt we'll ever actually see that happen in my lifetime.

I played the old Eidos Thief games a while back so when this re-roll popped up on sale, I figured I would give it a try. Results were mixed.

Thief opens with the protagonist, Garrett, interacting with Erin, his junior-sidekick thief on route to their current "big score" (the journey to said big score also serves as the game's tutorial). Things go poorly and Garret wakes up a year later, with no memory of what had happened.

Gameplay has two aspects: story chapters in their instanced areas, and a sprawling city rife with guards, apartments, and loot, and client (side) missions. Of the two, I found the latter much more enjoyable. The controls of the game (WASD, E action button, etc) are simple, though at times, slow to respond. Sometimes it felt like it took me several keystrokes to jump, even standing in the same place, or to switch types of arrows. Even so, I generally found little difficulty moving around the city. I enjoyed that the city was fully three-dimensional, meaning the player can run and jump across the rooftops, looking for places to break in and things to loot. Guards and city watch patrol the streets but as one might expect, they rarely look up. The F key allows Garrett to "focus" which will highlight loot, traps, threats and other interesting items. Focus is a limited resource but can be recharged with the right items.

Though the player can move around the city at their discretion, and at their own pace, the chapter/mission areas are much more linear and tend to have pretty much one path to the finish. Some of the chapters are interesting, like the one that involves seeking an underground ruin buried under a working whorehouse, which had a good balance of sneaking, looting, and puzzle-solving; other chapters are more standard and less exciting. (On that note, there is some nudity in the game, and some bloody violence, so not a game for children.) There are also extra missions the player can take on between chapters, with decent rewards. In both city and missions/chapters, there are literally hundreds of pieces of loot laying around. It's fun trying to find them all. There are lots of locks to pick, traps to avoid, and equipment upgrades to buy.

The player will encounter guards, sentries, revolutionaries, and thugs, and other beasts in the course of the game, though other than some non-human opponents, they were all pretty much re-skinned versions of the same foe. Combat is weak and uninspired, but then Garrett is not supposed to be a great face-to-face fighter, and does better firing arrows from stealth. He can employ water arrows to put out torches, rope arrows to climb to high areas, blunt arrows to turn switches or break gears, and broadhead, sawtooth, and fire arrows to slay foes and set stuff on fire. There are even blast arrows, which provide a satisfying explosion to kill multiple foes (if clustered) at once.

All that might be okay, if the guards were not pains in the ass. I don't mean for Garrett, I mean for the player. Their detection range felt *highly* inconsistent. On occasion, they would get stuck and spin in place, stop their patrol routes (sometimes reloading is the only way to reset them), or alter their routes on the basis of where the player is. The spinning and glitching is sloppy, the change of pattern is just lazy game design to artificially raise the level of annoyance. Add to that the freak monsters, which are basically unkillable in melee. If they detect you and you don't have fire arrows, you're reloading. And like most of these types of games, even if the player murders a guard in plain view of another one, and escapes, the guard won't raise a general alarm or anything but will soon go back to patrolling as if nothing happened, sometimes stepping over the corpse of his squadmate to do so. This may be an anti-frustration feature, so players can still sneak through that area later but it stretches the bounds of credulity. That's to say nothing of the conversation and phrases they repeat ad infinitum. Two guards will talk about becoming "a rat show" (ie, being a corpse and being left for the rats) or a roll in the hay with Polly Adler, repeating the conversation again and again and again, sometimes immediately saying the first line of the speech to start a new cycle before the last line of the previous round was spoken. Further, NPC dialogue volume is all over the place, sometimes sounding like the guy is on top of you even though he's two streets over. As I said, very sloppy.

The graphics and sound are fair without being earthshaking, though I noticed some mistimed audio with the characters speaking in cutscenes. Voice acting was ... passable. I did enjoy the rendering of the city, in all its Gothic dreariness. In general, though, I have to say the game was stable. I never had any crashes and load times were brief.

There are optional objectives in the chapters/missions that are varied but have no margin for error. Missing a single piece of loot (of over a hundred in some cases) or one opportunity to headshot an opponent will fail a secondary objective and this is frequently in areas where you can't backtrack. Completionists will find this infuriating. I made it through without much supply trouble, except the game wants you to use so many goddamn rope arrows Garret should be able to carry twenty-five of them. Upgrade your quiver capacity ASAP and do not start a chapter without your quiver full if you care about getting all the collectibles and loot or you most likely get into a spot where you just can't get them all--not that you won't be able to take a shortcut but not reach them, period--which reflects poor level design.

The story and characterization are serviceable but riddled with familiar cliches and all of them are played straight: the brooding loner, the spunky sidekick, the helpful associate that keeps the loner supplied with gear and info, the strategically-placed vendor(s), the well-intentioned zealot, the eldritch relic that threatens the word, peasant revolution, and so on. And please tell me why does every game I play lately seem to have one horror survival level ... and this one is set in (of course) an insane asylum. It's tired and I wish they'd stop.

I got about 80% of the Steam Achievements. Some are easy and will come naturally through a normal run; others require doing things like picking up easily-missable collectibles in areas you can't backtrack to unless you replay the whole chapter ... so if you want to maximize achievements, maybe consult a guide early. Some require playing all the way through with personal handicaps, such as not killing or knocking out a single opponent or using your focus skill for the entire game. I wasn't invested enough to try another run.

I sank 65-ish hours into Thief in one partial playthrough, decided to start over, and played to the end. I spent more than half that time swooping around the city, pickpocketing guards, doing the side missions, and assembling collectible sets ... but by the end of chapters, I was just going through the motions, because the fun was sucked out of the game by a bland story and annoying level design. This is the lowest score I can give a game and still recommend it and I *do* recommend it, because I enjoyed the non-story content a fair bit, though I see no replays in my future. I advise you wait for a sale to try it. I did, and got my money's worth.

Pros
- Enjoyable sneaking and stealing simulator, open world city movement
- Amusing, varied side missions

Cons
- Blah story missions with wildly inconsistent design
- Erratic, annoying NPC behavior

From my perspective, your experience with Thief (2014) will depend strongly on the expectations and experience you go in with - experience either with older games in the Thief series or with Eidos Montreal games, such as Deus Ex - Human Revolution. I've played the latter, not the former, and I enjoyed Thief. There are criticisms, of course, which I will get into.

But first, the positives - I really like the art design. The world has a dark, grimy, moody feel, and while any evaluation of graphics is highly subjective, I love the level of fidelity in this game. I've not seen any glitches or textures that failed to load/ loaded distorted, and there is honestly nothing I would change about the game graphically. 

The music is great. From what I've listened to, the music of the original Thief served mostly as a background piece, amplifying the mood that the map and lighting and environment was creating. Here, though, the music seems at times to serve its own purpose, and I enjoy music that has the confidence to do that. It is emphatically NOT only background music, even though the music is generally never interfering with stealthing around.

The sound effects are crisp, I like the overall feel of the menus, it's never really confusing how to navigate the options and Log, and for me, the controls were great. Overall it's really satisfying to swiftly glide between shadows, and avoid patrols and light alike. I should add, though, there's a slight camera wobble that took me some getting used to. Generally in FPS games the player model wobbles, while the world seems relatively smooth, like on a dolly. But here the entire world wobbles along with Garrett. Might not be your style, but that's how it is.

Finally, there are some stellar moments in terms of traversal and variety of movement - there's plenty of fun to be had in walking right over the heads of patrolling guards or gangsters and I enjoyed getting up there, or down in some sewers, or on some ledge, or just on the ground, along a shadowline. Verticality adds a great new dimension to this game.

Now, for the criticisms, with the mildest ones first - the story is not really engaging, and while it does throw around some surprises, the characters are only just about likeable enough to justify tolerating the story. It's never really thick, it never really grabs me, and I call it the mildest problem since the game isn't about story, it's about stealth and theft. [spoiler]It was really nice, though, to have a final "boss battle" where you still had to be a thief and not suddenly become a combat wizard.[/spoiler]

Second - the major side quest chains end abruptly and pretty badly. In fact, absolutely none of the side quests have any consequence on the game world that I could notice. [spoiler]For example, Ector's quests lead to a "working automaton" but we never see or hear anything about this thereafter. I was hoping I would have some automaton soldiers on my side that I could deploy at some point, but nope[/spoiler]. The side quests that Basso offers are also cookie cutter fetch quests, with barely any offering up unique challenges and interesting maps. Meanwhile the side quests in Deus Ex HR not only meant something significant to the characters involved, but also made some difference over the length of the story. Plus, NONE of them were simple fetch quests.

Finally, my biggest negative on this game, no questions asked - the map design. After Deus Ex: HR, it became clear that Eidos Montreal could create immersive, deep and carefully designed game worlds to support an almost endless variety of builds, emergent gameplay, and creative solutions that even they may not have anticipated. That masterpiece was basically a sandbox - you're given a goal, and your approach is absolutely not limited at all. You choose the approach, and see organic in-game rewards or punishments for it. It never felt like a puzzle, you actually felt like Adam Jensen trying to figure out how he could best face this situation given the skills that he had.

Thief feels like a puzzle - in many side quests, especially, there is literally only one way to approach the goal. There were so many occasions where I looked up to see if there was a bar to use a rope arrow on - nope. I tried seeing if there was a vent somewhere, to plan an escape route - nope. I searched for some kind of object to throw to cause a distraction - nope. Credit where credit is due, the later levels significantly picked up the complexity of the map, the opportunities to traverse the environment and the density of the level design - but for the most part this basically mean that stairwells on opposite ends of a corridor met up through one semi-hidden path. The interconnectedness that we saw all through DE:HR was almost totally missing. There was no opportunity I could recall of the game surprising me in terms of the map and gameplay mechanics, whereas in almost every DE:HR mission you would come to the final objective and realize there was a much simpler way of getting there which you didn't even consider. 

This would not be a criticism if some random studio had produced this game. Hell, if Ubisoft had developed this game I would be praising them for the map design. But knowing that Eidos Montreal had also made the stellar DE:HR and would go on to make the brilliant DE:MD, this game falls short of being somewhere in between, and is neither a successfull follow-up nor a predecessor to either of those titles.

With that said, if you're looking for a linear game, with a load of sneaking around, some combat mechanics which I never really bothered with, semi-decent map design and a smattering of lore and in-game documents to collect (as well as a truckload of in-game loot collectibles, that was a nice touch) then you can't go wrong with Thief. But don't go in expecting anything similar to the Deus Ex games or the other Thief games. You'd be missing out on a competent first-person thieving simulator then.

[h1]Things I Liked[/h1]

[b]Smirky the Thief[/b]
Garrett still has some wry wit here and there, and a couple of his lines made me chuckle. Overall though, I liked old Garrett better. The new one just tries too hard to be Mr. Broody Man, and it's a bit disappointing.

There's also some wit sprinkled throughout the story. I particularly enjoyed a bit where Garrett needed to trail a drunk named Lenny on a side mission. I really wish the game had more of that.

[b]Figuring It Out[/b]
There are a few puzzles to solve and, though most are far too easy, a couple are actually interesting and take some keen observation to work. They were very enjoyable.

[b]Difficulty Customization[/b]
I was entertained with how hard I could make the game for myself - turning off options for take-downs and kills, and those for upgrading Garrett's equipment, and the like. The game felt better once the difficulty was upped significantly. It is possible to play utterly stealthy, with no help, and still get through it all, which (to me) is the strongest point in its favor.

[b]Graphics[/b]
The graphics look great and there's fantastic atmosphere in some of the levels. The graphics don't need to be as good as they are, but it makes some stuff interesting to look at and explore - but I'm afraid that the other side of that is that the great graphics might why the levels are so small and there are so many, many load screens. I'd take less great graphics over more time spent watching things load, though.

[b]Stealing [i]Everything[/i][/b]
Yes, this is fun. I like looting and scavenging games, and perhaps that says something about me, but there's a lot of in here, and I enjoyed it thoroughly.

[h1]Things I Didn't[/h1]

[b]The Tiff-Taffing Language[/b]
Taff is gone, and that's incredibly sad. One character mentions it, wondering what the word means, but in general the NPCs use "adult" level language and like to drop the f-bomb. It feels unnecessary and gratuitous in a Thief title, and didn't lend anything to the game.

Besides that, they needed a good editor. There are grammatical mistakes in everything from the loading screen tips to the dialog, and sometimes they're weird and glaring (such as people asking a question in one tense, and being answered in another) and sometimes just distinctly non-native speaker in phrasing. I expect more from a company this large.

[b]The Story[/b]
The story makes a kind of sense. Sort of. But what it feels like is five different people wrote five different stories with different subtext and meanings, then they cut the different stories into strips, put them into a hat, and drew parts out as they needed something else for Garrett to do with his time. There's no unifying voice at all, and there are some times you just go "That makes no sense whatsoever." The end is beyond unsatisfying, so don't look for any resolution or epiphanies there.

[b]The Boss Fight[/b]
No one plays Thief for a boss fight, you taffing idiots.

[b]The Sound[/b]
I don't know what they did with the sound for this game but it's an utter failure. Half the dialog is either very loud, or so muffled you can't hear it at all, and distance to the speaker doesn't seem to make any difference - subtitles are pretty much a necessity. Even then, the game is plagued with conversations amongst NPCs that repeat ad nauseam, often so quickly that the same NPCs are having the same conversation four times simultaneously. Even if whatever they're talking about is something you've already dealt with and you really want the game to stop telling you about it.

Be prepared to hear that "Jebediah Chokes is a right prick" so often that Garrett (that's you) may snap and kill every NPC in the zone just to [i]MAKE IT STOP[/i]. Not that that's what I did, or anything. [i]Nope[/i].

[b]E is for Everything[/b]
Playing Thief, I got incredibly sick of mashing the E key. E is, variously: open a chest; open an armoire; open a door; open a drawer; pick a lock; pick a pocket; read a document; pick stuff up; peer through a keyhole; open a window; pry with your crowbar; enter a zone transition; enter a "squeeze point"; move a beam; unscrew some bolts; open a grate; cut out a painting; disarm a trap; hide behind something; open a safe; set a pin while picking a lock; enter a cabinet; rappel - and likely about fifteen other things I've missed in this list.

About half the time, the pressing of the E key seems wholly unnecessary. For example, if you want to open a window, you long-press E. Then Garrett will look around the window and get out his crowbar (the same animation every time), and then it wants you to tap E to cause Garret to pry the window open. Except, [i]why does it matter[/i]?  There's no way to "fail" opening the window, no way to make noise while doing so, no way to jam it if you don't use the right rhythm or anything, and no way to cancel out of it - you just tap E repeatedly and it opens. Why am I tapping E again?  Is this some trick to make me think I'm doing something when really all I want is for the animation to end and let me move on already?

Beyond that, with E for everything, you will invariably encounter confusion. You wanted to snatch that silver flask off that crate quickly and step away?  Sorry, we're going to make you crouch and peek around the crate it's sitting on instead. This kind of thing gets old really fast. I've been playing mouse-and-keyboard for a long time and would really like the single action button concession to console-based players to go die an ugly death now, [i]thank-you[/i].

[b]Abandon All Hope[/b]
The levels are riddled with points of no return, with zero warning that's what they are. When this happens, it feels as though the game is punishing you for exploring, which is totally not what a Thief game should be doing.

[b]Loading...[/b]
There are way too many load screens. How a game like GTA can go without them, and you can't get two streets over in Thief without a load screen I can't figure. The worst part is that you don't always know when you're going to trigger a load screen. Hey, that window - could be a flat to rob: you'll never know until you sit through the repetitive window-opening animation, and bam! Load screen. [i]Sucker![/i] Didn't mean to leave the zone and need to go back to the old one now?  How about you sit through that animation and load screen again. This is fun for you, right?

[b]See Monkey Climb?  Climb, Monkey, Climb![/b]
There are points in this first-person game when suddenly the camera changes to third-person view, and you're forced to maneuver Garrett up some pipes and around some ledges in this third-person view as if you're suddenly playing a platformer. It's really disconcerting, and I was annoyed every time it happened. There really didn't appear to be any point to these - there were no enemies to avoid, no jump you could miss, and only one path to take. No idea what these sequences were about nor why anyone thought they were fun or a good idea.

[h1]My Recommendation[/h1]
If you're looking for a game, well this is one, and if you can get it on sale, go for it. Play it as a stealth game, up the difficulty, and don't even try to get involved in the story. But if you're looking for Thief, this isn't it.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Thief[/i] is one of those games I hesitated to play because of all the mixed reviews, but now that I’ve finally given it a fair shot… I’m kind of obsessed. No, it’s not perfect. Yes, it deviates from the classic [i]Thief[/i] games in meaningful ways. But when it’s working—which, for me, was most of the time—it’s a rich, tense, atmospheric stealth experience that knows exactly how to reward curiosity, patience, and planning. This is a stealth game where your eyes are constantly darting between shadows and guard patrols, where you mentally map every route, where the simple act of cracking a safe in a dark room feels like the most thrilling thing in the world. It’s moody, immersive, and often beautiful, even a decade later.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Stealth that feels rewarding. [i]Thief[/i] isn't your typical modern AAA action game where you can charge into a room and beat everyone up. You're a thief. You're supposed to stay hidden, avoid people, and disappear before anyone realizes you've been there. Sneaking across rafters, putting out torches, picking locks, and slipping past guards feels fantastic.

[*] Satisfying level design with strong verticality and multiple routes. While some levels feel more constrained than others, many of the best missions offer a wide variety of paths, secret entrances, vents, balconies, and environmental tricks to manipulate. You feel clever for discovering an alternate route through a window, or for finding a hidden crawlspace that bypasses an entire patrol. 

[*] The atmosphere is immaculate. This version of The City is grimy, gothic, and drenched in sickly candlelight and fog. You can almost smell the soot and mildew. Everything from crumbling tenements to opulent manors feels handcrafted with incredible texture and lighting work. Even just walking the streets, eavesdropping on conversations, or slipping through windows builds a vibe you want to sink into.

[*] Fantastic stealth toolkit. Water arrows, choke arrows, rope arrows, noise makers, lockpicks are all thief fantasy tools brought to life. Figuring out which tools to use and when is half the fun. I also appreciate that you can turn off or reduce the HUD if you want a more immersive experience.

[*] Stealing stuff feels weirdly good. The little animations of Garrett picking up coins, examining jewelry, and cracking safes add a surprising amount to the experience. It isn't just a matter of walking up to an object and watching it disappear into your inventory. There's a tactile quality to it that makes every little bit of loot satisfying to collect. Yes, I will absolutely risk my life for that one extra coin.

[*] Strong sound design and environmental storytelling. Listen carefully, and you’ll hear guards humming, civilians gossiping, or wind blowing through broken shutters. Read a scattered note, examine a suspicious setup in a room, and piece together the lives of people long gone. 

[*] Underrated replay value. With side jobs, challenge modes, and plenty of loot and secrets you’ll almost certainly miss on your first run, [i]Thief[/i] invites you to return with a sharper eye. Trying to ghost missions, go full kleptomaniac, or find all hidden paths gives the game legs far beyond its main campaign.
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Garrett’s rebooted personality is kind of a letdown. He’s serviceable but lacking the wit and world-weariness of the original games. He delivers dry one-liners and seems oddly detached from the plot, like he’s annoyed to be there. The story wants him to be a brooding anti-hero, but he ends up feeling flat compared to his legacy.

[*] The main story is a mess. The supernatural plot never really comes together, Erin's character arc is confusing, and all the stuff involving the Primal feels like an excuse to string the heists together. I honestly enjoyed the game much more when I stopped worrying about the story and focused on sneaking around and stealing things. 

[*] Rope arrow system is strangely limited. One of the most frustrating design choices: you can only use rope arrows in pre-designated spots, even when there are tons of other wooden beams or surfaces. 

[*] Middling combat that feels more like a punishment than a tool. If you get caught, your options are… run, blackjack, or pray. There’s no real combat depth or skill expression, just sluggish parrying and a clunky swing. 

[*] Some players may bounce off the slower pacing. If you're looking for flashy, fast-paced action or constant story beats, [i]Thief[/i] may feel too slow or methodical. It’s a game about watching, waiting, creeping, and sometimes… just listening.
[/list]

So you play as Garret, a 'Master Thief' in a city where the Baron’s Watch spreads a rising tide of fear and oppression.
You progress through the story sneaking behind the shadows of city, stealing as much valuable loot as you can as quietly as possible. This is a game that is not your friend if you prefer to go full carnage-mode rather than stealth-mode. If you're not into stealth games, this is not the game for you.

MY LIKES:
The stealth system is where Thief works best. I really liked the swooping mechanic using the space bar that allows you to dash 10ft forward that really made Garret feel like a ninja. The parkour felt smooth and effortless. The graphics looked great. As a puzzle-lover, I really loved the puzzles and lock-picking opportunities the game presented you with and I really wish there was more of it!
I absolutely loved the chapter where Garret explored the asylum. Based on this chapter I felt like Thief also had a great potential to be part horror-game as well if it wanted to be. Aesthetically, the visuals and sound effects in the game were very limited, although wonderfully ambient for the setting that it was trying to portray.

MY DISLIKES:
An issue that I had with some of the levels in this game is that they're small and so...empty-feeling. Some levels are even smaller than the levels that are in Dishonoured. Speaking of Dishonoured, this game felt too much like it was trying to be Dishonoured. 
The guards are pretty dumb and easy to exploit. As long as you keep yourself within the shadows, doesn't matter if you're just two feet away from the face of a guard, they somehow don't manage to spot you. Their field of vision is very limited and even laughable at times. Even if they do happen to spot you, there is no challenge in running away from them. If you play this game, crank up the difficulty mode to Master Thief or you won't have any challenge beating the game.
When it comes to the story of the game, the narrative was fairly bland, filled with rather dull and under-developed main characters (including Garret).
While the parkour felt smooth and effortless, it was pretty inconsistent at times. Places where you feel like you should have been able to climb or jump on oftentimes were not an option. 

VERDICT:
Overall I found this game to be pretty fun for a stealth game. I personally found the story to be pretty unsatisfying, (especially the ending) but other than that I really did enjoy the core game.
I bought this game when it was on sale for $7, and I would say it's definitely worth it for that price. I would say that the game is even worth it for $20. Anything more than that price I would argue to be a bit of a stretch.
I give this game a solid 6/10 👍

First of all, if you're a huge fan of the original Thief series you should approach this game with caution because...

Storyline

And the main drawback is Erin. Erin is a bottomless bag of cringe and a poor excuse to advance the story. Also, most of the things from original series are not in this game, but yea, spin-off.

Gameplay
Surprisingly, gameplay is pretty fun if you can look beyond stupidly long animations of opening and closing drawers/closets/doors ets. Because if you're trying to collect most of the loot from a chapter, be prepared to sit through those again and again and again. The levels are pretty well-designed and you have lots of tools at your disposal to approach different situations (if you remembered to buy those tools). The stealth system is good and you have instant feedback if you're standing in light or darkness or if someone is beginning to spot you (audio clues included), sneaking past enemies is rewarding and so is finding a completely different route through the level. Secrets are well-hidden and if you're going for 100% it's gonna be challenging to find them all without a guide. I tried really hard to like this, and with 21 hours in the game, I almost finished it. But with about a dozen side jobs left and two last story missions to go, I just couldn't do it. Traversing the city in this game is so tedious and boring, that I began to view opening the game with dread.

There are things to like:
- the stealth is quite satisfying, such as using shadows and swoop
- the graphics are beautiful and the voice acting is quite good (although FPS drops were common)
- lots of side jobs in addition to the main story
- the game is quite 'tactile' in the sense that you see the main character's hands a lot and gives a good immersive feel

The biggest problem is the level design which is just so bad. It is incredibly disappointing as this game could be amazing, but the more you explore, the more you hate exploring. There are nonsensical invisible walls everywhere. There are many places you should clearly be able to jump or climb, but the game severely limits your pathing and your routes become too linear. This is disappointing as the main areas you move through become bigger and bigger, but you just end up walking the same boring paths over and over. There are almost no places to really be creative about how you will move about, yet SO much of your time is just spent moving through the city, especially as there is no fast travel system (ordinarily, I don't like fast travel in games like this but because your movement and exploration are curtailed, I found myself wishing for it).

There are some interesting places to explore in the city, and it is fun discovering lots of little hidden areas with nice loot. The problem is that the linear pathing discourages exploration as you know that you are just going to be using the same two or three (and sometimes even one) way of getting places, and that you will be running into ledges, roofs etc. that you should definitely be able to climb, but the game decides you can't. Apparently, you can climb this box here, but that's not possible for this IDENTICAL box on the next street over.

There are also lots of loading screens even in relatively small areas. They are disguised, such as you opening a window and climbing through into the new area. Sometimes, you don't know if the window you are opening is really taking you into an interior, or loading you into a new area, which can make traversing the maze-like city confusing. The map you are given is poorly laid out, and for some inexplicable reason, none of the areas are named.

I will say that the poor level design doesn't always extend to the story missions, which do sometimes allow for more creativity. Unfortunately, the majority of your time is spent in the city. The most disappointing thing is that the game actually gives you some pretty good stealth mechanics and options for lethal and non-lethal takedowns - it just doesn't let you really explore them as you wish, due to the poor level design. Also, even in the mission stories, there are no options. You can walk in through the front door, the balcony or the basement maybe, but those are the extent of your choices - the objectives or how to approach them offer no variety.

If you don't care about being able to move freely and don't mind linear movement with little room for creativity, then give the game a go. The rest of it is pretty good if you go in with low to medium expectations. For me, it was just too limiting and by the end of Chapter 6 (there are 8 in total), I was just so bored of moving through the same areas in the same ways over and over, I just had to stop. If you do want a game with better level design and more freedom (and a better story), try Dishonored.

I think they left it out because if you weren't  forced to re run the same parts of the map.  The game wouldn't have even been 15 hours of play time.  Speaking of which, I beat it in 20 hours and I was not trying to go fast.

NPCs are painfully boring and I started killing them just so I didn't have to hear them talk anymore. It was the same 5 conversations recycled over and over again. I also got real tired of the *grab loot* animation, or when  you pick up a collectible (which there are too many of) there's an animation you're stuck in - you want to run or go back crouching? Too bad!

The 'main' characters were also...meh. And the storyline could have used some polishing. Considering this was a Square Enix and Edios game like...you had the money.

Here's what I would have done - spoilers for the story ahead-

First off, the I didn't care about Erin. We met her for all of a few seconds and she was annoying. Instead of starting out trying to break into the Baron's mansion, let's start out breaking out Basso. You also could meet the special clients at this point, who are also looking for Basso - maybe letters in his office, or NPC talk. 

You start out the game finding out that Basso has been arrested. This is an issue for Garrett and Erin because no Basso means no jobs. You go to Basso's last known location to find some clues, and that's were you meet Orion who hints at a big job but needs Basso. You go to the Beggar Queen for some info, she tells you he was arrested by the General and is now in the tower. Garrett and Erin realize they need to know how the tower is laid out, so they decide to break into the architect's mansion.

During this time, you're learning the controls by traveling the city, which has been opened up. There are more paths, more platforms, because this a Thief game. 

You get to pick - play Erin, who's more combat focused, or play Garrett, who's more stealth. From there, you do the architect's mansion level. You give options - paths for Erin and Garrett. Only Garrett has the wrench and wire cutter, and Erin has the claw - there are paths only meant for one of them, and paths that both could reach. 

You get the plans, now it's tower time. It's not on fire (yet) and Garrett talks to Erin about the legendary treasure vault. Again, you get to pick your player and travel the tower. You get Basso, you decide to look for the treasure vault, the part plays out the same - inside the vault is the book this time. Garrett is obviously disappointed, but it must be worth something to someone - Basso will know. 

You return to Basso, get some side jobs, and get hired to do Orion's job - steal the ring. Again, you get to pick your player, you crawl through the graveyard, meet the General - basically the same story. 

By now you've gotten attached to Erin - she's there, you can play her, we have character development - she's learning from Garrett, mellowing out, we're learning about her past, so on. 

This is when we get the job to go the Baron's mansion and Erin gets fused with the gem. Now you do the 1 year jump where Garrett wakes up to a sick city and blah blah blah. We want answers - we go to Basso. We assume Erin is dead, but we still want to know wtf happened. Basso tells us the General is a frequent flier at the brothel, and hey - there's also a hidden library there that could tell you more about that Gem. So we do the Brothel quest, find clues about the Primal, meet the corrupted humans, get a vision from Erin ,so on. 

Next is the Asylum which....they tried. They really did on that level, they tried to make it scary. I'll give them props for it. Returning from the Asylum, and realizing Erin is still alive, we get re-introduced to Orion who wants the primal stone fragments. Orion tells Garrett Erin might be back at the Tower, because hey - it is a prison, but with the riots getting worse it'll be dangerous. Basso also tells you that the legendary safe has been redesigned by Clockwork (one of the special client sidequest guys) so it's worth checking out. 

We return to the tower, now on fire. Paths are different because it's falling apart - this is fun because it's the same place, but the map is different. We don't find Erin, but she was here - we get one of those vision segments pointing us towards the vault. The vault is now a puzzle the shifts and such, but there are other ways to solve it because it's a Thief game. Inside is a piece of the stone, the General is there, we banter, we dip.

At this point, we don't know where Erin is so the only thing to do is to talk to the Baron, and we also need his Primal piece. Chapter plays, riots cause map changes, so on. This map needed more paths - we could have had servant's passages, panic rooms, hidden architecture, more lore...a lot of potential lost. It's an old manor - use it. Anyway, we get the stone, find out about Orion, find out about Erin, so on. 

From there we proceed to the Hidden City and the ship. And we fix the last encounter, because man...was it some BS. We go from Erin throwing a tantrum to a young girl, angry and confused at the world and how she's been treated. She's been tortured, held captive, and has this horrible power inside of her. She also has guilt, guilt at the people she's corrupted and the city she's killing. We help Erin fight herself - this is going to be a teamwork fight. Set the boat on fire if you want - it's wooden, and the primal is angry. Use the environment to create some tension. 

And then if you want to do the shitty "I'm slipping" ending go for it, I'd prefer a more loving "Sibling love wins" ending where Erin and Garrett both realize you need other people to help solve your problems...you know, character growth.

🔰SHREDVIEW🔰 - From someone who actually plays and finishes the games before reviewing.

NOTE: If you like my work, please check out the rest of my reviews, I put a lot of work in these to offer the best overall description of what you’re up against. Thank you in advance!

🔷 ABOUT THE GAME & LORE 🔷

In the 2014 Thief reboot, Garrett, the master thief returns to a plague-stricken City ruled by a d**khead. He’s hired to steal a book from a mysterious figure named Orion, who claims to hold a cure. What our guy uncovers is a deeper conspiracy involving the Primal, a power behind the plague and a stir in the revolutionary undercurrents of the City. He must stop the Primal from being unleashed and unravel who’s pulling the strings in the darkness.

The City is dark, Gothic, steampunk-tinged, full of shadows and secrets. The Gloom infects the populace, the elite isolate themselves, and Garrett walks that thin line, profiting from chaos while navigating the moral ambiguities. He is more of an anti-hero; a thief doing what a thief does but gets pulled into saving a broken world anyway. Well, you can’t steal if you cease to exist, right?

🔷 THE GAMEPLAY 🔷

👉 GENERAL:
This is a linear action-stealth game done well. It’s not open world, levels guide you but it gives enough room to roam, steal, hide, and manipulate darkness in large areas. The story drives your missions by chapters and in between you get to pad your pockets, pick apart locked rooms, and become better at what you do. I think Dishonored 1's success in early 2012 inspired a new perspective on this classic title. The aesthetics, world atmosphere and character design feels similar.

   •	For it's age, it still holds up to expectations. I've finished it in 2023 and didn't feel vintage yet, I actually enjoyed it and it's also decent to look at. However, it's gameplay and mechanics all tailored towards stealth are what makes Thief a special experience.

   •	Your best friends are your tools, especially your bow for which you have multiple arrow types, each with different purposes and functionalities. There is also a progression system through upgrades, which you can acquire by earning good score and loot in levels. Nothing crazy, easy to master as a game and difficulty is challenging enough but delicate, it won't drive you insane even at it's worst. 

   •	Kill or no kill is a real choice. There’s an achievement for non-lethal playthrough, and the game leans toward you being better off staying in shadows rather than spilling blood. 

    •	The whole game is a skill mastery training course, you'll learn a lot about how to generally move and approach stealth in FPS video games, as well as train your patience and strategic thinking in situations. I found thief to be a very cool challenge loop of doing the same thing until becoming very fluent, sort of like martial arts. I think this is where it excels, again, everything is tailored around darkness and not being observed. 

    •	Difficulty and challenge balance is decent. It pushes you, but doesn’t demand perfection, unless you’re going for achievements. 

    •	The story is captivating enough, a decent fantasy steampunk inspired or somewhat gothic novel unraveling on your screen, controllable somewhat by your own hands. Thief is more of a book type game, it just gives that cozy feeling. Play this when it's raining outside and it's dark, with a window open, it slaps. 

👉 NAVIGATION SYSTEM:
You move through corridors, rooftops, shafts, vents. The City is segmented but connected via hubs. However, transitions are clunky and often interrupt immersion. One moment you’re sneaking, next a loading screen hits because you passed through hidden geometry or shifting zones. Levels are segmented and sometimes it kills freedom of movement.

👉 PHYSICS & MECHANICS:
Mechanics are solid just sometimes may not behave exactly as you expect. Hitboxes sometimes betray you and the AI can be dumb or ruthlessly precise depending on the moment. Your Focus mode helps a lot. Use it. It highlighting paths, revealing routes, slowing time, etc. Weapons/gadgets feel great but not exceptional. 

👉  GRAPHICS & OPTIMIZATION:
For its age, it holds up. The aesthetics are moody, Gothic, steampunk dark fantasy. Good job on world tone. It looks fine in 2023 when I played it; I never felt like I was playing a relic. But cutscenes, lighting mismatches, and texture pop-ins show seams. The game in general visuals is solid, not mind-blowing. The gameplay is core.

👉  ACHIEVEMENTS & COLLECTIBLES:
These are the real beast. They are doable but semi-missable and some require perfect stealth, knowledge of maps, paths, gadgets. You may need guides to catch everything. I got 100% in 63.2 hours in order to carefully get everything in one playthrough while taking my time exploring every nook and granny. S**t. I meant cranny. 

🔷  CONCLUSION  🔷

“Thief (2014)” is a lean, stealth game that doesn’t overpromise but delivers enough to satisfy fans of shadows and quiet takedowns. It’s flawed AI, loading screens, occasional mechanics hiccups are observable but it still nails the feel of being a ghost in a dark world. If you love stealth, you’ll find parts of it enthralling. If you want depth or freedom, you’ll want more. It’s a very nice exercise, I’d say. You should try this. 

🔷  PROS & CONS  🔷

-	Stealth mechanics are solid and mood is dark and immersive.
-	Tools and gear give you options without overcomplicating.
-	Kill/no-kill choice adds replay value.
-	Skill mastery loop is very satisfying.
-	Still looks good for a 2014 title.

❌ CONS:
-	Level segmentation and loading breaks immersion.
-	Combat and animations sometimes misbehave. 
-	AI can be inconsistent.

Dear fellow thieves,

I don't know where to start. Where... to start the rant.

Gameplay:
This game is way to easy. The guards that shall defeat you are dumb as nuts. Oh, don't forget they might see you from time to time through a solid wall and kill you without seeing them.

So, after the fall of Looking Glass Studios and all those years later, everyone wanted a remake, or a fourth installment in the series. So everyone was hyped after the announcement and what do we get? One of the most average games in video game history. Nothing more, nothing less. It really is a shame to destroy so much potential and one of the best stealth series out there! Reminds me a lot of the third installment, but the third game offered some fantastic lore at least. So let's break it down a bit.

1.) Story and Characters

Well what is there to say. If you think of it as some sort of remake, then they managed to waste all of the potential of the first 3 installments. It's loosely based on the lore of all three games, but they really didn't pick up any of the great elements from back then. In return they made a rather boring, uninteresting and generic story out of it. Same goes for the lore and the characters. While Garrett is still great, all the other protagonists are not memorable at all and lack some heavy background. Even more so for the antagonists. While i still have the pictures of Constantine and Karas in my head, i have a hard time remembering the ones from this game. Even though I just played trought the whole thing. Plus, most things don't make any sense at all. Why, for example, does the general appear in the strangest places for no reason and much more. I don't want to spoiler here, so see for yourself.

2.) Level Design and Gameplay

While I understand that balancing a game like this is not easy. On the one hand, you want to get the sneaky part right and, on the other hand, you want to give the main character something to defend themselves. As in the first three games. Priority on the sneaky stuff ofc. There is nothing wrong with that. But somehow they managed to make the game extremely easy. Even on master difficulty, with custom options. Playing as Predator is very easy and playing as ghost is even easier. When you not going for all the loot you can rush trought the game in 3-5 hours. That brings us to the next problem.
So if you're looking for the loot and the secrets, it adds around 30-40 hours of game time. And yes, I understand. The game is all about secrets and loot. But that's about 80-90% of the game time, just for random collectibles, random loot for money that you never really need as you can easily beat the game with no upgrades and without most consumables. Also some random jobs and side missions that don't really add anything lore-whise and aren't that much fun, besides some side missions. Most of the time when you are in the city you run like a madman from a to b, to c, picking the lock for the 5th time and opening the window for the 7th time. This is ok for a while, but it gets boring and tedious very quickly and only artificially lengthens the game.
One last thing here. The mission design is pretty good, but when you think of some of the most memorable missions in the first two (three) games, they fall flat here. Just think of Constantin's mansion, the prison and the lost city. Or the bank, the tower, and the ambush in the second game. Also the cradle in the third. All of these secret rooms, shortcuts, traps made a lot more sense and been actually fun to discover. Here .... not so much.

3.) Graphics

The graphics are quite nice for the time, but the cutscenes look like the mid or late 00s, rather than 2014. And using the same character model all over again for the black market dealer is just plain cheap. The same applies to the transition from one zone to the other. The one with the beam. How can you use the same transition about 20 times a game? It's like using the exact same exact model of a tree for the Vista, in Assassin's Creed III, 10 times or more. It's just extremely stupid.

Conclusio:

Long story short. As I've said several times, the game is perfectly fine. Maybe not if you're a huge fan of the first two games, but I had fun anyway. At least for a while. I just played a lot for all the achievements. Otherwise I would have played a lot less. I think it's not nice to rant about a 7 year old game, but some things just have to be said. ^^
So, if you've never played a Thief game before, get it on sale for a few couple of hours. For those who played the old games, rest assured. You don't miss anything in terms of story and lore. Let's hope for another restart of the series in about 10 years. And i hope it is a better one.

Personal score: 5.5/10

An unmitigated and unbridled disaster of a game. I bought it for less than 2 pounds sterling and still feel ripped off. How they managed to ruin almost every aspect of this game is beyond me.. it literally blows the mind. The gameplay design decisions are an affront to gamers everywhere. They have effectively removed any sense of freedom from the player, almost as if you, the player, cannot be trusted with even the most simple of tasks - moving from point A to B in a way that suits you best? No, you will move down the paths designated for you to move. Jumping? Who needs that. It's too loud anyway and you'll attract the attention of the braindead guards. Would you like to use a rope arrow? No, you can only use it in the 3 places in the entire map designated for use with a rope arrow. Even something as simple as falling off a ledge of my own accord was impossible! Traversing through the "open world"? Laughable. This.. collection of claustrophobic tunnels punctuated with the most obtuse load screens (some activating as soon you unknowingly open a window) was a miserable experience. Looting? Have fun looting ink wells and kitchen spoons netting you a grand total of 2 pieces of gold. I shouold mention that EVERY single action you take is a quick time event. Opening a door, looting a cupboard, climbing through a grate, scratching your thieving ass.. all time-consuming and repetitive visual events that add nothing to your overall experience but serve to delay you from completing your action of choice. How fun. I could go on and on with how atrocious it actually feels to play, the lousy storyline, abysmal level design, the lack of Garrett's original voice.. the horrendous audio mixing and repetitive NPC lines you're graced with over and over again, but alas I would be wasting even more time than the 3.3 hours I could bear to play. What a horrible way for such a legendary series to go out.. if you haven't gathered already, avoid at all costs - even if that cost is 2 pounds sterling. You're a gamer god damn it, and you deserve better than this drivel.

If you are expecting a Thief sequel, this is not it. Check out Gloomwood instead.

This is a love story. You play as Gary the Thug who gets friendzoned by the love of his life Erin when he refuses to murder random civilians for a dollar. She then gets kidnapped by a rich man like the gold digger she is and you spend the rest of the game stealing cheap common everyday items to be able to afford a tier 3 sub to buy back her respect for you.

All my favorite things in 1 game. Super atmospheric 1900th century urban stealth looter with a touch of the supernatural to keep things interesting. I could (and did) spend hours (17 straight hours) just wandering around looting random buildings. If you liked playing Dishonored, this game is for you.

It’s hard to recommend Thief 2014 when Dishonored does a spectacularly better job with the same ideas. It’s hard to recommend Thief 2014 when the original Thief trilogy remains much more unique and engrossing.

Thief games were the antithesis to fast-paced FPS action games, emphasising slowness, quiet, immersion, exploration, nonconfrontation, improvisation. Someone thought what was missing was a chase scene, QTE loading screens, linear level design, combat reticles, irritating sidekicks, surreal dream sequences, and more explosions.

This reboot throws out all the interesting worldbuilding and mythology of the originals, only to make something bland and forgettable, that never really gels or finds its own identity.

The new voice actor tries hard but can’t replicate Russell’s effortless charisma. But mostly it’s the writing that lets him down. Old Garrett had a pithy wit, this one just has an attitude and states the obvious. His character is poorly developed; he’s less a cynical idealist than an emo teenage rebel. I loved his base in a clocktower, but why does he have exhibition boxes for rare collectibles? Doesn’t he need to sell these to make a living - isn’t that the point of being a thief? Any Robin Hood credentials falter with every poor person’s hovel he ransacks for jewellery and spoons.

The writing is lacklustre throughout. One of the joys of original Thief was overhearing guard conversations, but you won’t find much of that here. The guards sound bored, and their lines might be literally “I’m so bored” or similar. They have so little to say that their conversations repeat maddeningly often, sometimes to the point where several guards will speak identical lines simultaneously, creating a hilariously creepy echo effect. Ditto for notes, they rarely build to anything interesting.

To call the story convoluted would be understatement. Flashbacks and flashforwards, amnesia and missing time, mystical artefacts, persons dead yet alive, psychic links…that’s just the first mission. Rarely did I have a clear idea why I was pursuing each objective, or if I did, it didn’t make logical sense. It seemed like a loose retread of Thief 1’s plot, but lacking all the worldbuilding that gave that story its payoff.

Original Thief encouraged non-lethal playthrough, but I didn’t feel any incentive for that here. Knockouts trigger animation so jarringly violent that I don’t think those guards will be getting up again. Being a stealth archer was more satisfying, more befitting the action game this wants to be.

Stealth/thievery mechanics are functional and absorbing. The game is mindlessly enjoyable when you’re just sneaking and thieving, not thinking about the bigger picture or little questions. Although I want to mention the occasional hilarious glitch where a guard would spin in circles. Turns out it’s very difficult to sneak past an enemy who is rotating 360’ a second. Another irritation was tapping E to lean out a doorway, which the game would often interpret as tapping E to shut/open the door, alerting the guards, the opposite of what you were trying to do. Audio levels were inconsistent to where NPCs were in relation to you, which is very disorientating in a stealth game, sometimes sounding like they were right over your shoulder when they were far away, or vice versa.

Visual effects were often the highlight. Rain effects were great, a section on a burning bridge, another in a lightning storm where flashes of lightning threaten to reveal you to the guards.

Of the original Thiefs, this most resembles Deadly Shadows, or rather the criticisms made of that game: small levels split by multiple loading screens, weaker plot, simplified gameplay, lifeless City hub; these criticisms that were maybe too harsh for Deadly Shadows feel too restrained for Thief 2014. Beholden to Deadly Shadows’ most unforgettable level, this Thief has also a scary level, and the excellent sound design deserves credit, making it one of the better levels here. But it can’t hold a flickering candle to The Cradle, and it’s nothing special amongst scary games.

While I found it dull and muddled but playable, ultimately Thief just made me angry. Why reboot a classic just to throw out all the best bits? If you don’t care about the existing fan base, invent a new IP - look up ‘thief’ in a thesaurus and concoct some generic stealth scenario. Dishonored solved this problem by devising a completely original world and style, and the result was an infinitely better game than this. The original games are all infinitely better than this mediocre fare. It’s the kind of thing that can make you angry about this autocannibalising culture of reboots and commoditisable IP.

Diet Dishonored, Thief in name only. The lore has been completely rebooted, Garret doesn't act like Garret at all, and everything story related is off.

Gameplay has more in common with Dishonored than the Thief series, with hub areas followed by more structured linear levels. Only in Thief '14, the levels are greatly simplified even compared to Dishonored. Gone are the massive (if fantastical) structures with multiple routes and complex objectives. The inventory has been incredibly simplified, rope arrows are incredibly scene specific (why does the wood beam need rope tied around it to be attached to?) It should have been taken out of the game if the developers didn't want to put any effort into it. Like moss arrows, which have been taken out for... what reason?

Ok ok, aside from comparisons to the namesake series, what about casual stealth fans. Honestly, fun can be had as such. The graphics are drab, but high quality. The swoop move can be fun, even if it almost breaks all of the stealth, and even though they are linear the maps can be decent, in a fun house ride kind of way.

The main game breaking flaw for me is the inconsistent traversal controls. Jump has been made context sensitive because... jumping is too complicated for modern gamers? Obviously not, more likely the designers wanted to make level design easier for the developers. I mean, okay? Whatever, I guess I could live with it, but in those context sensitive scenarios, you can never be certain if you are going to jump from one beam to another OR, in the worst design decision you could make in a stealth game, using the same key can have you jump off and go below. Wut? There is no reason this should be the same keybind. Movement in a stealth game needs to be a certainty. Having the context be ambiguous on whether you will jump across to safety or down into detection cannot be a problem in a stealth game. Jumping from a rope? Good luck on going where you want. Trying to drop from a rope, haha nope not gonna happen.

The game as is cannot be great, probably not even good stealth TBH, but if the major flaws could be modded then the game could be at least enjoyable in a mindless fashion. The game is locked tight, no modding.

I used to be disappointed in Thief 3, this game completely changed my mind on that game. This is like the Deus Ex Invisible War of the Thief series, only this killed the Thief series so far. Deus Ex lived on, in a lesser diluted version.

Play Thief 1-3, or Dishonored 1-2 if you are wanting a more mellow experience. This can be an alright $5 afternoon playthrough, but I can't fully forgive its flaws.

I didn’t play this expecting a true Thief game. Still, I will criticize some aspects from the perspective of it being part of the Thief franchise.

Things I disliked:

- Jumping system: It’s clear this game wasn’t properly tested before release. So many times I jumped unintentionally… So many times I wanted to jump, but had to take one or two steps back from a ledge just to make it work… And don’t get me started on how often I fell into pits even though I was holding the Run/Jump button.

- Same button for interacting and peeking: I just want to loot, and I end up peeking over a chest or a wall. So frustrating!

- The story makes no sense, and most characters are just annoying.

- False Master Thief: This guy gets caught so many damn times! He’s no Master Thief — he’s an impostor. He’s also a [spoiler]false Garrett. You find out in one mission that this game is a reboot, but somehow set in the future of the original trilogy. The original Garrett is completely disrespected by the creators in ways I can’t even begin to describe.[/spoiler] You probably missed this because the story and lore are so uninspired and forgettable, it’s not even worth reading the documents...

- Gameplay styles make no sense: They feel pointless. They could’ve been used to enhance difficulty or as a reward system in future entries. Also, in Chapter 7, one challenge is bugged.

- The game killed the original concept: Everything was made generic and “modern” (like the map system), and it feels like the game is meant to be played with a ridiculous amount of assistance. Even Garrett’s voice reflects that — constantly explaining everything to you, as if you’re dumb. (Though, to be fair, you can turn this off in the options — thank God.)

- The mechanics aren’t fluid: Almost everything you do is a trigger for a short cinematic. Takedowns, jumping, looting, opening things, interacting — you’re not really playing, you’re just watching animations. I assume this was done to make the game feel more modern or realistic, but it just feels bad.

- Terrible shadow system: The light gem (or whatever it is now) is completely unreliable. Sometimes you’re in a dark area and fully exposed; other times you’re in a lit area and somehow hidden. It makes no sense.

- Sound system and quality are awful.

These last two points alone are enough to kill the game for me. If you’re making a Thief game, these two systems — dynamic shadows (with a reliable visibility gem) and 3D sound — are absolutely essential. And this release completely failed on both fronts.

As a stealth/action-adventure game, it’s just weak.

I know I’m about 11 years late with this, but I had to state the obvious. Still, I managed to 100% the game — I’m a completionist.

Verdict: Only worth buying on sale.

I'm an old hat Taffer. I've been with the series since it started, and I'm not ashamed to admit up front that my review is biased. I have played Thief TDP and Thief TMA to pieces and back and then some. I also enjoyed Thief 3 and while in the end I must admit it was a fairly respectable game in its own regard and I also enjoyed it for what it was. In the origional games you had free reign of the city, go where you please when you please, even if it was something utterly asinine like becoming a member of the rootop climbers guild (some of you may know what I mean, others may not) or seeing if you could jump out of the map or just screwing around looking in every nook and cranny just because you could. This new reboot of Thief, or Thief 4 rather (though I shudder to think of it as part of the series I love) is nothing more to me than a regular run of the mill game that is nothing special or even that good, and a cash grab. 

There is no jumping in Thief so far. Yes, you read that correctly. You are GLUED TO THE GROUND. A real throw back to when I played FFXI and FFXIV online. At one point there are a pair of floor traps early in the game that any reasonable human being with half a brain could jump over, and for our acrobatically gifted Garrett should be no problem to jump. As you can't jump, you have to take a predesignated route around the traps instead of just jumping over them. Do you want to go up a wall? You need to hold spacebar and can only climb in designated spots. Do you want to go up or down a ladder? If so, you need to hold spacebar until you have a mini cutscene happen (and it IS a mini cut scene, as your character takes control of himself to turn around and face the ladder then takes a few steps onto the first rungs when going down, or takes the first few steps  by himself to latch on before you can go up) and you actually get on the ladder. There is no more auto latching on ladders (a crime in itself) and it becomes a nuisance and frustrating to have to hold a button to get onto a ladder, and then become glued to said ladder until you either reach the top or bottom. Did you enjoy rope arrows and their magical ability to catch on ANY wooden surface in the past? Guess what kids, designated spots only!

Speaking of mini cutscenes, lets talk about mini games that serve no purpose. If I want to open a window, I hit "e". But wait! We need a mini cutscene where you pull out a crowbar and have to tap "e" a few times to open the window. Or move a beam from inside the gap out of the way. Another tap "e" moment to make me waste time. The character is completely automated in his movements in both going through the window and gap sliding, so why are you making me tap "e" at all. Either let me open the damn window in one smooth fluid motion without having to play a tap "e" minigame, or skip the stupid cutscene and just let me interact to open the window and mantle through as I please. Same with being forced to move objects out of the way.

I can't speak for the story yet. When I (sadly) finish the game - and I know I will I will likely update my review. So far though all I can safely say is they've used a few throwback names older fans recognize to try and appeal to them. To be fair as well, they added back in things we asked for like rope arrows. They added in options to turn all of the new flashy hand holding garbage off. They added options to make the game as difficult as some of us are used to. It's not enough. The game is just flat out bad to me because it feels so much more restrictive than previous games. It does have a very Thief 3-esque feel to it, but it just hasn't jived with me at all even several hours into the game. 

On another note, I was more than ticked off at not being able to collect a collectable in a side mission as apparently the game adds a few required tools - in this case a razor and possibly others- to loot specific items -in this case a painting. Unfortunately for me the side quest to do this mission becomes available BEFORE you can even purchase the razor, so if you want to get that collectable then tough luck, you can't go back to that area again later in the game (so far at least) to get it, it seems to be lost to the ages. Not very wise game design there in my opinion. I hope I'm wrong and at some point you can go back because this pissed me off to no end, and I don't normally fluster easily.

By the way, I was on the fence the entire time about buying this game, especially after seeing it at E3. I decided to try and give it the benefit of the doubt and buy the Master edition of the game. Imagine my complete and utter shock and surprise today to see that there is already DLC for the game, and not only that if you paid the extra money for the game, you don't get all the DLC, just one called "The Opportunist". Really? Seriously, REALLY? The extra mission comes no matter what version you buy, and I couldn't give a damn about digital art or soundtracks or TF2/DOTA items. I paid the extra to have the DLC, and then you put out more that isn't even included.

TLDR: If you only liked the first two games of the series and hated Thief 3 its a definite don't buy. If you enjoyed Thief 3 then you may also enjoy this, though it is far more constrictive than past games (not such much Thief 3 which was also fairly linear in it's own way, but definitely 1 & 2 where you could pull off some fun and amazing things by going where you shouldn't and/or getting out of the map.) on where you can and can't go (notably because every rope arrow and jump is in a predesignated spot). Removing something as small as the ability to jump when and where ever you want really killed this for me, it takes away a freedom you don't know you've lost until its gone.

I really, really wanted to love this game but I just can't. :(

I genuinely don't get the hate this games gets. Yes it's not the immersive sim from '98, but it's got the most hardcore stealth scoring system I've ever played. What would be considered a ghost run in other stealth games is a whole new category here under "Opportunist" which means you dared using the environment, like a material man!
